facts: The Douro makes about as much table wine as fortified wine.
The region has three subregions, from west to east: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo and Douro Superior.
Baixo Corgo has the mildest climate and most rain, Cima Corgo has the most vineyard and centered on Pinhão, and Douro Superior is the hottest and driest.
The Marão and Montemuro mountains shelter the region from Atlantic winds, giving a continental climate with hot, dry summers and cold winters.
A royal Portuguese charter of 10 September 1756 defined the Port production region, one of the world's first formal wine demarcations.
Port is made under its own DOC, Porto, from the same area, while the Douro DOC covers the unfortified wines.
Younger Madeira blends, typically three and five years old, are heated artificially by the estufagem process, while older colheitas and frasqueiras use the canteiro method.
Canteiro ages the best wines in cask using only the natural warmth of the barrel storage rooms, for many years or decades.
The four major white grapes, from sweetest to driest, are Malvasia, Bual, Verdelho and Sercial, and Terrantez is regarded as a fifth noble variety.
Tinta Negra is the dominant red grape, used for approximately 85% of Madeira, and since 2015 it may be named on the label.
Colheita Madeira must be at least five years old before bottling.
Since EU regulations of 1986, at least 85% of the grapes in a Madeira must be the variety named on the label.
Port is made by adding grape spirit, called aguardente, to stop fermentation early, which leaves residual sugar and gives about 19% to 22% alcohol by volume.
Port comes from the demarcated Douro region, which has three official zones: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo and Douro Superior.
The primary categories of red Port are Ruby, kept in tank to preserve color and fruit, and Tawny, aged in barrel with age indications from 10 to 50 years.
Vintage Port is made entirely from the grapes of a declared vintage year, spends a maximum of two and a half years in barrel or steel, and ages for decades in bottle.
Late Bottled Vintage is aged in barrel and bottled between four and six years after the vintage, and it may be filtered or unfiltered.
Colheita is a single-vintage tawny Port aged for at least seven years in wood, with the vintage year printed on the bottle.
About 86% of Vinho Verde is white, fresh with natural acidity, around 8.5 to 11% alcohol, and slightly sparkling, usually from artificial carbonation today.
Alvarinho and Loureiro are the two most successful white varieties, with Alvarinho giving low yields and high alcohol and Loureiro giving higher yields and very aromatic wines.
The DOC has nine subregions, which may appear on the label with the name Vinho Verde, such as Vinho Verde-Amarante.
Stellenbosch was first planted in 1679, and makes about 14% of the country's wine.
The district is ringed by the Helderberg, Simonsberg and Stellenbosch Mountains, with soils from decomposed granite on hillsides to sandy, alluvial loam in the valleys.
The Stellenbosch wards are well known for red wines, particularly Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinotage and Shiraz.
A strong wind called the Cape Doctor blows through the Cape wine regions, limiting mildew and fungal disease and tempering humidity.
Some 88 percent of Spanish production comes from only 20 grapes, including the reds Tempranillo, Bobal, Garnacha and Monastrell and the whites Albariño, Airén, Verdejo, Palomino and Macabeo.
Vino de pago (VP) is a category formed in 2003 for high-quality, single-estate wines, where pago means a vineyard estate.
Only wines made by the traditional method may be labelled cava, and other sparkling wines may only be called vi escumós.
About 95% of all cava is produced in the Penedès area of Catalonia, and the two major producers are Codorníu and Freixenet.
Macabeo, Parellada and Xarel·lo are the most traditional cava grapes, and Chardonnay and Malvasia are also permitted.
Authorized red grapes are Garnacha tinta, Monastrell, Trepat and Pinot Noir, and rosé cava must be made by the saignée method, not by blending.
Spanish winemakers officially adopted the term cava in 1970 to distinguish their wine from French champagne.
Palomino makes about 90 percent of sherry grapes, and Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel are used for sweet wines.
The best vineyards are on albariza, an almost white soil that keeps moisture through the hot summer and suits Palomino best.
Fino and Manzanilla age under a layer of flor, while oloroso develops no flor and oxidizes as it ages.
Amontillado is first aged under flor and then exposed to oxygen, which makes it darker than a fino but lighter than an oloroso.
In the solera system, wine moves through several tiers of barrels, so most sherry carries no vintage, and VOS and VORS mean at least 20 and 30 years average age.
Priorat is one of only two Spanish regions with DOCa status, alongside Rioja, and is called DOQ in Catalan.
Its soil is llicorella, a base of reddish and black slate with small particles of mica that reflect sunlight and conserve heat.
Garnatxa negre is the traditional grape and is found in all the older vineyards, with Cariñena, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah also authorized.
Yields are very low, usually far below the authorized maximum of 6,000 kg/ha, because the rocky soil does not hold water.
Vineyards are planted on terraced slopes at altitudes between 330 feet and 2,300 feet, with hot, dry summers and cold winters.
Reserva wines must remain 12 months in oak barrels and then 24 months in bottle, and Gran Reserva wines 24 months in oak and then 36 months in bottle.
Rías Baixas is a DO in Galicia, granted in 1988, which replaced the Denominación Específica Albariño status given in 1980.
Albariño represents over 90% of all vines planted, and over 90% of the wines produced are white.
The DO has five sub-zones: Val do Salnés, O Rosal, Condado do Tea, Soutomaior and Ribera de Ulla.
The climate is Atlantic, with wet winters, sea fog, high rainfall and mild temperatures, and summer maximums rarely exceed 86°F.
Vines are trained along granite posts called parrales, with wires, to protect them from humidity and maximize summer sun exposure.
Condado do Tea is the warmest sub-zone, with summers sometimes near 104°F, cold winters and rainfall of over 79 inches a year.
Ribera del Duero is a DO on the northern plateau of Castile and León, founded on 21 July 1982, and it has stayed a DO rather than becoming DOCa.
Wines come almost exclusively from red grapes, and the vast majority is Tinto Fino, the local name for Tempranillo.
Tinto Fino is often complemented with Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec and Merlot, and Albillo is the only authorized white variety.
Vineyards lie between 2,460 and 2,989 feet in a continental and Mediterranean climate, with about 18 inches of rain a year, summers up to 104°F and hard winters.
Aging rules match Rioja: Crianza needs two years with 12 months in oak, Reserva three years with 12 months in oak, and Gran Reserva five years with two in oak.
Rioja is a DOCa, the highest category in Spanish wine regulation, and in 1991 it became Spain's first DOCa.
Rioja has three zones: Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa and Rioja Oriental, which was formerly called Rioja Baja.
Rioja Alta is higher and gives brighter fruit and lighter wines, Alavesa gives fuller body and higher acidity, and Oriental is warmest and driest and often used for blending.
The traditional red varieties are Tempranillo, Garnacha tinta, Mazuelo and Graciano, and the traditional whites are Viura, Malvasía and Garnacha blanca.
Aging takes place in 225-litre oak barrels, and red Crianza needs two years in total with at least one year in barrel.
